transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:05] Priya Kumar: priya here, lead ml.
[00:07] Tom Reynolds: tom, infra.
[00:09] Evan Lee: evan, cto.
[00:12] Ben Ortiz: ben from redwood, se.
[00:14] Hannah Park: hannah, ml research.
[00:18] Maya Chen: cool, goal for today is a deep dive on GPU runtime profiling - kernel selection, tensorrt-llm vs vllm, and how cuda graphs fit into our capture and replay strategy. we'll surface tradeoffs for latency vs throughput and quantization.
[00:34] Priya Kumar: sounds good. our background: we're running mixed chat workloads at ~1800 rps peak, lots of short seq len (avg 64) but tail up to 1024 for docs. p99 latency target is 250ms for hosted use, but for private on-prem we can tolerate higher if cost drops.
[00:52] Tom Reynolds: infra constraints: air-gapped on prem, nvidia h100-sxm and a couple a100s. storage is fast nvme, kubernetes cluster w/ gpu nodes and internal registry. mentions about sso and audit logs later.
[01:12] Ben Ortiz: okay great. a couple quick framing points: vLLM tends to be more flexible for dynamic batching and prefix kv cache sharing across requests; TensorRT-LLM gives potential kernel fusion and int8 accelerate with trtexec profiling, but graph capture and replay (cuda graphs) can change latency characteristics.
[01:36] Priya Kumar: quick q - in your experience, when does tensorrt-llm actually beat vllm for short seq workloads? we care about latency at 64 tokens.
[01:50] Ben Ortiz: short answer: depends. if you can fuse kernels and your model fits quantized kernels well, TRT-LLM with cudagraphs can shave 20-40% off p50 latency. but for highly dynamic sequences and many different prompt shapes, vLLM's continuous batching and kv cache reuse keeps the p99 lower because it avoids repeated graph recompile overheads.
[02:16] Hannah Park: are we seeing miscompiles or kernel thrash when switching seq lens? like sudden slowdowns?
[02:22] Ben Ortiz: yeah, we see that a lot. when runtime picks a kernel based only on current batch shapes, a sudden seq-len jump causes different kernel selection and sometimes kernel launch overheads spike. CUDA graphs help by capturing the common exec path, but if the path deviates you either re-capture or fall back to non-graph path - which adds jitter.
[02:46] Maya Chen: ben, could you quickly explain how we profile kernel selection? what traces we need from customer?
[02:52] Ben Ortiz: sure - we need per-op kernel names and timings (nvprof/nsys traces are good), sequence length histograms, batch-size distribution, and kv cache hit/miss traces (we collect prefix hit ratio over time). ideally also memory allocator logs and GPU utilization. with that we can map hot ops to kernels and see which kernels dominate time or memory.
[03:18] Tom Reynolds: we can run nsys in our air-gapped env but need the exact invocation.
[03:22] Maya Chen: i'll share the exact nsys command and a sample script.
[03:28] Priya Kumar: also on quantization - we tried int8 on a 7b model and saw hallucination rate go up. how do you balance that with latency gains?
[03:40] Ben Ortiz: that's the classic tradeoff. our approach: 1) run quantization-aware evals on your eval set (we'll run quality regressions tied to prompts), 2) use mixed-precision or per-layer quant at first (only quantize MLP layers), 3) compare token-level perplexity and end-task quality. sometimes int8 on some layers with fp16 on attention gives most of the latency upside with minimal quality loss.
[04:02] Hannah Park: can you show any numbers from previous pocs? p50/p90/p99 shifts?
[04:07] Ben Ortiz: yes - we have a slide but high level: for Llama-3-8B on h100, vLLM fp16 with continuous batching: p50 38ms, p90 120ms, p99 320ms for short seq. TRT-LLM with graph capture + int8: p50 22ms, p90 75ms, p99 420ms in one customer's workload - note p99 worsened in that case because of different prompt shapes and re-capture costs.
[04:37] Evan Lee: that's interesting - lower median but worse tail. could caching the prefix kv help p99?
[04:43] Ben Ortiz: yes, prefix kv cache is huge. if you can cache the KV for repeated system prompts or long contexts, you avoid recomputing earlier layers. vLLM's cache sharing is built for that; in TensorRT setups you can persist KV but the mechanism depends on your runtime and memory. also quantization interacts: cached KV in int8 might need different storage layout.
[05:07] Priya Kumar: what about cudagraphs specifics - we run with variable batch sizes, will graphs still help?
[05:16] Ben Ortiz: cudagraphs shine when you have a stable execution path: fixed batch, fixed seq-len path, and identical kernel sequence. For variable batch sizes we either maintain a small set of captured graphs (per batch-size/seq-len bucket) and dispatch the closest one, or fall back to non-graph. But managing a large graph cache increases complexity.
[05:38] Tom Reynolds: managing graph cache in k8s - any tips for memory?
[05:42] Ben Ortiz: pre-allocate GPU scratch pools, use unified allocator, evict least-used graphs, and instrument eviction thresholds. also track GPU memory fragmentation - cudagraph capture can increase fragmentation if captured transient allocations stay pinned.
[05:59] Priya Kumar: can you explain kernel selection plumbing - how does runtime choose kernels across tensorrt-llm and vllm?
[06:08] Ben Ortiz: broadly: runtimes profile op shapes and hardware capabilities. vLLM focuses on flexible kernels (custom fused attention kernels, flash attention variants) and dynamic code paths; kernel selection happens at op-level based on heuristics (seq-len, head dims). TensorRT-LLM relies on TensorRT's optimizations and fusion passes - it picks kernels that maximize throughput via tensor core fusions. The key is the heuristics: small head dims or odd seq lengths sometimes pick suboptimal kernels.
[06:36] Hannah Park: are there runtime flags we should try? like limited autotune or force kernel X?
[06:41] Ben Ortiz: yes - both runtimes expose flags. for vLLM you can pin attention impl (flash/megatron) and batchersize heuristics; for TRT-LLM you can set workspace size, tactic selection or disable certain tactics. We usually run a few autotune passes and then lock tactics for production to reduce variability.
[07:02] Maya Chen: let's walk through an example - customer provides a model, we run a baseline vLLM fp16 run w/ nsys, then run TRT-LLM with graph capture and int8 to compare. Ben, what artifacts do you produce?
[07:13] Ben Ortiz: we'll produce per-op flame graph, kernel timeline, sequence-length heatmap, and a latency distribution breakdown (p50/p90/p99) plus memory maps. We'll also provide a suggested config file: batching thresholds, graph buckets, quant config.
[07:30] Tom Reynolds: how intrusive is TRT conversion? we have custom ops in our model serving stack.
[07:36] Ben Ortiz: conversion can be intrusive if custom ops aren't supported; we either add plugins or keep those ops in fallback (vLLM path). For many standard transformer models it's straightforward. We'll know more after you share the model.
[07:50] Priya Kumar: what about warmup cost for cudagraph capture - does that add a long tail when capacity scales up?
[07:58] Ben Ortiz: captures take time and memory. strategy: warmup ramp (prepopulate graph cache during scale-up), keep a small pool of warmed GPUs, or use async capture in background while serving at reduced QPS. There's an operational tradeoff: warm GPUs cost money.
[08:20] Evan Lee: any thoughts on autoscaling with graphs? we use k8s cluster-autoscaler.
[08:26] Ben Ortiz: when new nodes spin up, you need warmup. autoscaler policies should include warmup windows and node pools with reserved capacity. Redwood Dedicated offers burst pools for this pattern, but on-prem you'd orchestrate a warm pool.
[08:42] Maya Chen: Priya, can you share your seq-len distribution now?
[08:45] Priya Kumar: sure - average 64, median 48, 75th 120, 95th 560, 99th 980. Many short chat turns, occasional long doc-summaries.
[08:58] Ben Ortiz: with that tail, I'd recommend a hybrid approach: use vLLM fp16 for baseline low-latency path and offload long seq or heavy-batch throughput tasks to TRT-LLM batches with cudagraphs. Also keep an LRU KV cache keyed by conversation id.
[09:18] Hannah Park: about KV cache - are there pitfalls with long-lived KV entries? memory leak risks?
[09:23] Ben Ortiz: yes, need eviction policies and TTLs. Also when quantizing, the storage format differs and you might need to recast KV during recall which costs time. We track cache hit ratio and cost per hit during profiling.
[09:41] Tom Reynolds: can we store KV on host memory to reduce GPU footprint?
[09:45] Ben Ortiz: yes but then recall latency increases; you can keep hot keys on GPU and cold keys on host. For h100 there's good memory bandwidth so often worth keeping more on GPU.
[09:58] Priya Kumar: show us a sample nsys capture and what to look for - Ben?
[10:03] Ben Ortiz: (screen share) you'll see kernel launch bands, memcpy ranges, and periods where kernels serialize. Look for long memcpy gaps and kernel queues piling up. Also check for tactics: if one kernel dominates e.g., radix sort or softmax, that's a target for fusion/optim.
[10:25] Priya Kumar: sometimes we see weird 'unknown' kernels in traces - is that due to vendor naming or custom plugins?
[10:31] Ben Ortiz: often plugins or JIT'ed kernels show as unknown. we correlate with op-level timelines and sizes.
[10:37] Evan Lee: any gotchas when we cross-compile from dev to prod - dev uses a100 and prod h100?
[10:43] Ben Ortiz: yes different tensor core ops and tactics. You should test on prod hardware; tactic selection may differ. We recommend running a small matrix across hardware types.
[10:54] Tom Reynolds: what's the best way to bucket graphs? by batch size or seq-len?
[10:58] Ben Ortiz: usually by effective compute shape, so combine batch*seq and group prompt templates. For example buckets: {batch1-len64, batch4-len64, batch8-len64, batch1-len256, batch4-len256...}. Keep only top 6-8 buckets to limit complexity.
[11:18] Hannah Park: are there automated tools for managing graph caches?
[11:21] Ben Ortiz: some frameworks have community tools; Redwood has internal tooling to suggest buckets automatically from seq/batch histograms and capture them during quiet periods. we'll share that.
[11:30] Priya Kumar: okay, want to talk about quantization again - which quant scheme is most reliable? static calibration or per-channel?
[11:38] Ben Ortiz: per-channel symmetric quant is usually more reliable for weights. Activation quant can be tricky; static calibration with representative data is best. Also consider GPTQ-like post-training quant for large models.
[11:53] Tom Reynolds: does TRT-LLM support GPTQ or similar?
[11:58] Ben Ortiz: there are plugin paths; it's evolving. sometimes you run a conversion step pre-deploy. We'll test on your model during the POC.
[12:07] Maya Chen: security/on-prem notes - Tom mentioned air-gapped. any constraints for profiling?
[12:13] Tom Reynolds: can't upload traces externally. need to share results via secured channel; we can run scripts locally and export sanitized artifacts.
[12:21] Ben Ortiz: that's fine - we'll provide self-contained profiling scripts that produce sanitized artifacts and a RedTeam-approved template.
[12:29] Priya Kumar: during POC; will Redwood help with conversion?
[12:33] Ben Ortiz: yes, our SE team will help with conversion, plugin builds, and run benchmark harnesses.
[12:40] Evan Lee: SLA question - if we go TRT-LLM path and see p99 spikes, what mechanisms do we use for graceful degradation?
[12:48] Ben Ortiz: multi-tier routing: keep a fallback vLLM path for tail requests; route by request-size or latency budget. Also implement circuit-breakers to avoid overload. Redwood runtime supports policy-based routing.
[13:03] Priya Kumar: want to see a specific example of routing by estimated compute.
[13:09] Ben Ortiz: (explains) estimate compute cost = tokens * hidden_dim * head_count heuristics; route small compute to low-latency pool and big compute to throughput pool. We'll provide routing rules.
[13:25] Maya Chen: let's capture the POC plan in one sentence and agree owners.
[13:29] Priya Kumar: sounds good.
[13:31] Ben Ortiz: plan: Redwood runs baseline vLLM fp16 trace on Peregrine's sample workload, then TRT-LLM with cudagraphs + int8, produce artifact pack, and recommend config for hybrid deployment.
[13:44] Maya Chen: owners? Ben, Maya, Tom, Priya aligned?
[13:48] Priya Kumar: yep.
[13:50] Tom Reynolds: yep.
[13:52] Hannah Park: quick follow-up on memory - we saw fragmentation earlier; any allocator prefs?
[13:58] Ben Ortiz: use pool allocator with big-aligned chunks, prefer cudaMallocAsync where available. For TRT capture, avoid transient small allocs during capture.
[14:12] Evan Lee: what's the expected runtime for Redwood's benchmark? how long till results?
[14:16] Maya Chen: 4-6 business days after we get the model and sample traces. Ben confirm?
[14:21] Ben Ortiz: yes, 4 working days to produce initial artifact pack and recommendation.
[14:26] Priya Kumar: okay we'll aim to share model by 2026-12-20.
[14:32] Maya Chen: any more questions on approach?
[14:36] Priya Kumar: one on monitoring - what metrics should we export to prometheus?
[14:41] Ben Ortiz: per-route p50/p90/p99, kernel-level ops/sec, kv cache hit ratio, GPU mem free, cudagraph hit ratio, quantization mode tag. We'll send a sample dashboard.
[14:58] Tom Reynolds: and logs for audits? we need to ship audit logs to our SIEM.
[15:04] Maya Chen: Redwood can push audit logs; we'll send the integration guide.
[15:09] Priya Kumar: any legal/compliance concerns with TRT on-prem plugins?
[15:15] Maya Chen: generally plugin licenses are okay but we'll include licensing notes.
[15:20] Evan Lee: let's wrap with a recap and confirm next meeting.
[15:24] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood to send profiling deck, nsys commands, scripts; Ben to run microbenchmarks once model arrives; Peregrine to provide model and seq hist, and we'll schedule POC kickoff week of 12/27. next meeting tentative 2026-12-28 for POC kickoff.
[15:44] Priya Kumar: thanks everyone.
[15:46] Tom Reynolds: thanks.
[15:47] Ben Ortiz: thanks, will follow up in thread.
[15:50] Maya Chen: end.
